title: Bounded contexts and domain events
idea: A bounded context is a boundary inside which each word has one meaning; a domain event is a past-tense fact one context publishes so others can react.
points: Sales and Warehouse may both say `Product` yet need different fields and rules.
Each context owns its model; contexts share only ids and small event records.
An aggregate records events like `OrderPlaced`; the application publishes them after saving.
Subscribers translate the event into their own model, so the publisher never knows them.

steps.caption: Three contexts, each with its own model. None imports another's classes.
A customer places order O-1. Sales checks its own rules inside the `Order` aggregate.
The aggregate records a fact: `OrderPlaced` with ids and values, never the `Order` object.
After the order is saved, the application hands the event to the bus.
Each subscriber receives the same fact. Sales does not know who is listening.
Warehouse translates it into its own model and reserves units on the shelf.
Billing reads only the total. Adding a Loyalty context later is one more subscriber.

code.title: The problem: one shared model
code.caption: Sales and warehouse share one `Product`. Receiving stock silently changes the shop price.

walk.text: One class for the whole company; `price` has no single meaning.
Sales code reads `price` as what the customer pays.
Warehouse code writes the supplier's unit cost into the same field.
Each team's code is correct alone. Together they corrupt the shop label.
No exception fires; the bug shows only as a wrong price in the output.

code.title: The fix: contexts + events
code.caption: Each context has its own `Product`. Sales publishes `OrderPlaced`; Warehouse and Billing react in their own terms.

walk.text: The event is an immutable record, named in the past tense, holding ids and values.
A tiny in-process bus. Handlers run in subscription order, so output is repeatable.
The aggregate records the event; `pullEvents` hands it over once, then clears.
Warehouse has its own `Product`: stock and cost, no sales price at all.
The handler translates the fact into a local change, or a backorder.
Publish only after the order is saved, or subscribers react to a rolled-back fact.

pitfalls: Putting the whole `Order` in an event couples subscribers to the publisher's internal model.
Publishing before the save commits lets subscribers act on an order that never existed.
Naming events as commands, like `ReserveStock`, hides that the publisher should not care who reacts.

quiz.q: Billing must invoice when an order is placed. What should `OrderPlaced` carry?
options: The Sales `Order` object so Billing can read any field
A reference to the Sales repository for lookups
Nothing; Billing queries the Sales tables directly
The order id and the plain values Billing needs
quiz.why: Plain ids and values are a stable contract. Objects, repositories or shared tables tie Billing to Sales internals and break the context boundary.

takeaway: One meaning per context; contexts talk through small past-tense events.

starters: How do I find where one bounded context ends?
